ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> Parents provided written informed consent, following the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki.

> Participants were further characterized by the presence of autism traits, evaluated by a certified clinician using the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule, second edition (ADOS-2; module 3) (48).

> The live video feed from each box was concurrently saved to disk and displayed on the computer monitor of the other box (scaled to be vertically filling, horizontally centered, thus maintaining the same aspect ratio), such that each participant had a direct view of the other participants' face and head.

> Upon entering the lab, participants were familiarized with the room and equipment.

> Finally, participants performed a 15-second validation task, during which participants were instructed to consecutively look at each other's mouth, nose and eyes for five seconds each.

> As a result, participants were unable to touch each other, and there was little opportunity for distractions or object-based interactions.

> The eyes of each participant are depicted on the other's screen at the same height as where the cameras are located, allowing participants to gaze at each other's eyes when looking straight into the camera.

Ethics approval statement:

> The Ethics Committee Research UZ/KU Leuven approved the study (S58807).

> Parents provided written informed consent, following the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki.

> This research was performed in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by 748 the Medical Ethical Committee of UZ/KU Leuven (S58807).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p > 0.19", "p > 0.23"), Sentence = c("All other interaction effects were non-significant (all p > 0.19).", "All other interaction effects were non-significant (all p > 0.23)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Background: Preterm birth has been linked to atypical social development and difficulties with social orientation similar to those observed in autism.
A fundamental component of social interaction is adequate gaze toward an interaction partner's face and eyes.
Preterm individuals have been reported to display atypical social gaze patterns, characterized by more frequent but shorter looks toward faces.

Methods: We compared looking times to the face, as well as eyes versus mouth during face-to-face interactions in preterm (N = 45) and full-term (N = 29) five-yearolds, using a video-based eye-tracking set-up.
Secondary, we examined number of dwells and mean dwell duration.
Each child participated in four interaction tasks, including silent looking at their mother, silent looking at a female stranger, and a positive and negative conversation with their mother.

Results: No statistically significant group differences were found between preterm and full-term children in percentage of total dwell times to either the face or the eyes, however small differences were observed with preterm children showing less dwells per minute with longer mean durations than full-term children.
We observed a marginal effect of interaction partner, with children spending proportionately more time gazing at their mother's face than at a stranger's face.

Conclusion: Preterm and full-term five-year-olds showed no differences in total social gaze to the face and the eyes of their interaction partner during face-to-face interactions, although subtle differences were observed in other gaze measures.
Speculatively, these findings may reflect a developmental catch-up in social orientation following initial delays in infancy.
Alternatively, advances in neonatal medical care, including infant-directed interventions in the neonatal intensive care unit, may have been successful in improving social gaze after preterm birth.
Given the context-dependent and individual nature of gaze behavior, these findings should be interpreted cautiously.
Future longitudinal studies employing consistent methodological approaches are needed to investigate how social gaze develops over time following preterm birth.
Atypical social gaze is one of the core characteristics of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) (1-3).
However, a range of other socio-emotional factors can influence the way individuals look at faces and eyes, including social anxiety, and emotional and behavioral problems.
Such difficulties are common following premature birth, highlighting the importance of investigating the development of social gaze in individuals born preterm.
Social gaze and eye contact are particularly important when interacting with others.

However, the field has only recently started to shift from studying social gaze in artificial contexts using static pictures or short videos of faces (4, 5), to studying gaze behavior during face-to-face interactions (6) (7) (8) (9).

text.text: This shift is relevant as gaze behavior has been shown to be strongly influenced by the presence and behavior of an interaction partner (10) (11) (12).
text.formatted: This shift is relevant as gaze behavior has been shown to be strongly influenced by the presence and behavior of an interaction partner <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(10)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(11)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(12)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, the presence of an interaction partner is crucial to properly investigate typical and atypical gaze toward faces and eyes.
Preterm birth is defined as birth before 37 weeks of gestation, and has many developmental consequences (13, 14).
text.formatted: Preterm birth is defined as birth before 37 weeks of gestation, and has many developmental consequences <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">14)</ref>.

text.text: As survival rates and physical health outcomes have steadily improved over the years, research has increasingly shifted to long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes.
Many individuals born preterm show a so-called preterm behavioral phenotype, characterized by heightened inattention, anxiety, and socio-emotional difficulties (15) (16) (17).
text.formatted: Many individuals born preterm show a so-called preterm behavioral phenotype, characterized by heightened inattention, anxiety, and socio-emotional difficulties <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(15)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(16)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(17)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, a three-tofour-fold increased prevalence of psychiatric conditions has been reported, most notably attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), ASD, and social anxiety (18) (19) (20).
text.formatted: Moreover, a three-tofour-fold increased prevalence of psychiatric conditions has been reported, most notably attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), ASD, and social anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(18)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(19)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(20)</ref>.

text.text: Research has demonstrated poorer social skills in individuals born preterm compared to termborn peers (21) (22) (23).
text.formatted: Research has demonstrated poorer social skills in individuals born preterm compared to termborn peers <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(21)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(22)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(23)</ref>.

text.text: These social difficulties might be related to reduced social preference or altered social gaze patterns (24).
text.formatted: These social difficulties might be related to reduced social preference or altered social gaze patterns <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(24)</ref>.

text.text: Several studies have reported that preterm infants orient less toward social scenes, faces and eyes (25) (26) (27).
text.formatted: Several studies have reported that preterm infants orient less toward social scenes, faces and eyes <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(25)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(26)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(27)</ref>.

text.text: In a recent review, we described a delayed and fluctuating trajectory of gaze behavior in preterm individuals (aged 0-5 years) during face-to-face interactions (28).
text.formatted: In a recent review, we described a delayed and fluctuating trajectory of gaze behavior in preterm individuals (aged 0-5 years) during face-to-face interactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(28)</ref>.

text.text: Overall, research suggests reduced gaze to faces for preterm infants compared to full-term peers (29) (30) (31).
text.formatted: Overall, research suggests reduced gaze to faces for preterm infants compared to full-term peers <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(29)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(30)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(31)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, this reduced gaze to faces seems to be characterized by a pattern of more frequent but shorter gazes (29, 32).
text.formatted: Importantly, this reduced gaze to faces seems to be characterized by a pattern of more frequent but shorter gazes <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(29,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">32)</ref>.

text.text: In other words, preterm infants look at faces more frequently but disengage more quickly, resulting in a shorter total looking time to faces.
This gaze pattern has been observed both in infancy and in later childhood, including in very preterm (gestational age ≤32 weeks) school-aged children (33).
text.formatted: This gaze pattern has been observed both in infancy and in later childhood, including in very preterm (gestational age ≤32 weeks) school-aged children <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(33)</ref>.

text.text: It has been proposed that these short, frequent social gazes in preterm individuals may reflect more immature attention regulation skills (29, 33) or may serve as a self-regulatory strategy during socially demanding interactions (32).
text.formatted: It has been proposed that these short, frequent social gazes in preterm individuals may reflect more immature attention regulation skills <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(29,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">33)</ref> or may serve as a self-regulatory strategy during socially demanding interactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(32)</ref>.

text.text: Evidence for altered visual attention following preterm birth has indeed been reported (34), suggesting a potential mechanism underlying these atypical gaze patterns.
text.formatted: Evidence for altered visual attention following preterm birth has indeed been reported <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(34)</ref>, suggesting a potential mechanism underlying these atypical gaze patterns.

text.text: Despite these findings, the preterm population is highly heterogeneous and findings are fluctuating, with a substantial proportion of preterm individuals showing social functioning and social gaze comparable to full-term peers.
For example, no differences in face-directed gaze were reported between preterm and full-term infants at 2-3 months of age (35, 36).
text.formatted: For example, no differences in face-directed gaze were reported between preterm and full-term infants at 2-3 months of age <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(35,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">36)</ref>.

text.text: Interestingly, Dean et al. (2021) reported reduced gaze to social information in preterm infants at 7-9 months, an effect that was no longer present at five years of age (37).
text.formatted: Interestingly, <ref type="bibr">Dean et al. (2021)</ref> reported reduced gaze to social information in preterm infants at 7-9 months, an effect that was no longer present at five years of age <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(37)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, Sekigawa-Hosozawa and colleagues (2017) identified distinct subgroups of very preterm children based on gaze patterns at social scenes, with one group exhibiting gaze patterns similar to typically developing full-term peers, and another resembling children with ASD (38).
text.formatted: Furthermore, Sekigawa-Hosozawa and colleagues (2017) identified distinct subgroups of very preterm children based on gaze patterns at social scenes, with one group exhibiting gaze patterns similar to typically developing full-term peers, and another resembling children with ASD <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(38)</ref>.

text.text: Overall, knowledge regarding social gaze following premature birth, especially beyond infancy, is rather limited.

Moreover, much of the existing evidence is either based on selected stimuli (i.e. pictures or short videos of faces) or based on observational studies of face-to-face interactions with time intensive manual coding.
While these approaches have yielded valuable insights, they either lack generalizability to behaviors in actual face-to-face interactions or they lack the spatial accuracy of eye-tracking methods.

The present study addresses these limitations by using a video-based eye-tracking set-up to investigate gaze toward the face and eyes during face-to-face interactions between five-year-old children and either their mother or a female stranger (i.e. one of the experimenters).

Specifically, we compared the percentage of time children spent looking toward the face (eyes, nose and mouth) versus the background, and toward the eyes versus the mouth, in preterm and full-term preschoolers across different interaction conditions.
We also investigated the effect of familiarity of the interaction partner, by comparing gaze behavior during silent looking conditions with their mother versus a female experimenter.

Silent looking tasks were chosen to minimize potential confounding effects of speaker versus listener roles on gaze behavior (39, 40), especially since these dynamics might differ between mother-child and stranger-child dyads.
text.formatted: Silent looking tasks were chosen to minimize potential confounding effects of speaker versus listener roles on gaze behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(39,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">40)</ref>, especially since these dynamics might differ between mother-child and stranger-child dyads.

text.text: We hypothesized that preterm children would show reduced gaze toward the face versus the background and reduced gaze to the eyes versus the mouth, compared to fullterm peers, and that all children would exhibit less face and eye gaze toward a stranger than toward their mother.

Lastly, we explored the potential confounding role of autism traits on social gaze by repeating the analyses while excluding preterm children with a formal ASD diagnosis or with clinically relevant scores on the Autism Observation Schedule (ADOS-2).

This research is part of the Resilience Study (41), which monitors preterm children born between 2016-2018 since initial admission to the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) at University Hospital Leuven, Belgium.

text.text: In total, 102 children (mean age 5.5 years) participated in the current study.
All children were native Dutch speakers with normal or corrected-to-normal hearing and vision.
The preterm group was recruited from the Resilience Cohort (41, 44, 45), and consisted of 70 children born before 37 weeks gestational age, with a birth weight below 2500g.

text.text: Of these, 37 were born moderate-to-late preterm (MPT; GA 33-36w), 21 very preterm (VPT; GA 29-32w), and 12 extremely preterm (EPT; GA ≤28w).
Children were excluded in case of major cerebral lesions (grade III-IV intraventricular hemorrhage, periventricular leukomalacia) or neurological conditions (cerebral palsy, epilepsy).
The comparison group comprised 32 full-term children, recruited through local schools, with a gestational age between 37-42w and a birth weight above 2500g.
None had a formal diagnosis of ASD or ADHD, nor a first-degree relative with either condition.
Furthermore, the full-term children did not stay at NICU or did not have any significant perinatal complications warranting invasive medical treatment.
The Ethics Committee Research UZ/KU Leuven approved the study (S58807).
Parents provided written informed consent, following the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki.

The experimental set-up (Figure 2) employed a two-way video configuration, adapted from Hessels et al.

text.text: The child and a female adult (either mother or female stranger) were seated in the same room, each in front of a wooden box containing a half-silvered mirror, which reflected the screen of a 23.8-inch LED-backlit LCD monitor using a resolution of 1920x1080 pixels lying at the bottom of the box.

A Logitech BRIO 4k Stream Edition webcam, placed at eye level behind the half-silvered mirror in each box, was used to record the respective participant's face and head at 30 Hz and a resolution of 800x600 pixels.

The live video feed from each box was concurrently saved to disk and displayed on the computer monitor of the other box (scaled to be vertically filling, horizontally centered, thus maintaining the same aspect ratio), such that each participant had a direct view of the other participants' face and head.
The latency between video capture and presentation at the other end of the set-up was 121 ms (SD = 13.9 ms).
Using the same calculations as in Hessels et al. (2017) (6), this means that the latency was below the minimum of 130 ms for noticing lag in speech-video asynchrony (50).
text.formatted: Using the same calculations as in Hessels et al. (2017) (6), this means that the latency was below the minimum of 130 ms for noticing lag in speech-video asynchrony <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(50)</ref>.

text.text: During video presentation, two Tobii Pro Spectrum eye-trackers, tilted at a 21.7° angle, were used to collect eye-tracking data at 600 Hz from each participant.
Light grey panels were placed behind each participant, ensuring a neutral background.
In addition to (dual) eye-tracking, the dyadic set-up enabled simultaneous recording of heart rate, brain activity, galvanic skin response and audio/video.
The current report focuses solely on the eye-tracking measurements of the child.
Upon entering the lab, participants were familiarized with the room and equipment.
Once they felt comfortable, they were seated in the dyadic set-up at a distance of 70 cm from the eye-tracker, such that one cm on the screen corresponds to a visual angle of 0.75°.
Using a height-adjustable table, the webcam in the box was positioned at eye height, allowing eye contact when participants looked straight ahead.
Daylight was blocked using window blinds and constant lighting was provided by diffuse artificial lights attached to the ceiling.
Once the participant was ready, a fivepoint calibration and four-point validation was performed using the Tobii Pro Lab software V1.171.
Next, children performed multiple tasks with their mother and a stranger, with the order of interaction partner counterbalanced.
Mothers were informed on the protocol prior to testing, ensuring procedural adherence.
The mother-child tasks included two minutes of looking at each other without any verbal interaction, and a three-to-five minute positive and negative conversation (based on Holleman et al.
Finally, participants performed a 15-second validation task, during which participants were instructed to consecutively look at each other's mouth, nose and eyes for five seconds each.
With the stranger, children performed two minutes of silent looking at each other, similar to the first task performed with their mother.
Data processing was performed using custom-built scripts in MATLAB R2021b (RRID:SCR_001622) and Python (v3.9.12; RRID:SCR_008394) in Spyder (v5.1.5; RRID:SCR_017585), unless otherwise specified.
The goal of our analysis was to quantify the time the child spent looking at the other's face and facial features.
To ensure adequate sensitivity of the gaze measures, we first performed several data quality assessments.
Eye-tracker calibration.
First, we checked the calibration quality of the eye-tracker to ensure high accuracy of the gaze point estimation.
The average calibration accuracy over the four-point validation was calculated per participant using a custom-built Python script.
A calibration procedure was considered good if the mean accuracy was ≤1.5° and the data-loss rate was ≤ 5%.

In the current set-up at 800x600 resolution, an accuracy of 1.5° corresponds to 40.5 pixels (~2 cm), which is approximately 2.5 times smaller than the area of interest radius of 100 pixels (see below).
Mean calibration accuracy of included participants did not differ between preterm (0.65° ± 0.29°) and full-term (0.61° ± 0.20°) children (𝐹(70.66) = 0.37, 𝑝 = 0.55).
Next, we estimated the amount of data loss per task to assess eye-tracker performance and participant's task compliance.
A data loss estimate was calculated by subtracting the total fixation duration over the task from the total task duration.

This means that any gaze behavior that is not a fixation (such as blinks, saccades, or fixations outside the screen), as well as any moment when the eye-tracker cannot provide a gaze estimate, is classified as data loss.

Head rotation.
Lastly, we wanted to differentiate between data loss due to participant behavior or due to poor eye-tracking performance.
Therefore, the participant's head rotation angles (i.e. pitch and yaw), as estimated by OpenFace 2.2.0 (52), were used to measure whether participants oriented their head toward the screen.
OpenFace reports head orientation angles in radian with the camera as the origin.

High eye-tracking data quality can thus be expected when the reported orientation angles are small, indicating that the participant is looking straight ahead (i.e. toward the camera behind the half-silvered mirror).
Based on the video data, a vertical orientation range of [-0.6 -0.6] and a horizontal orientation range of [-0.3 -0.3] was used as an operationalization for looking at the screen.
The proportion of frames exceeding the range for looking straight ahead in either direction (i.e. gazing away from the screen) were computed over the total amount of frames per video.
These proportions of gazing away from the screen were generally very low and similar for preterm and full-term children (Table 4).

text.text: Areas Of Interest (AOI) for eyes, nose and mouth were delineated using the Limited-Radius Voronoi Tessellation (LRVT) method (54), with predefined cell centers identified by OpenFace and a radius of 100 pixels.

The size of the radius was set to correspond roughly to the mean eye-to-eye distance of the female adults (95.8 ± 11.9 pixels), and roughly to 1.5 times the AOI span, with AOI span defined as the mean distance from each AOI cell center to the cell center of its closest neighbor (54).

Hereafter, dwells were computed using a custom-built python script.
Dwells were operationalized as the time that a gaze remains within a particular AOI, from entry to exit.
Therefore, a dwell may include multiple fixations and saccades within this AOI and short blinks.
The maximum time allowed between two consecutive fixations within the same AOI was set to 150 ms, based on estimates of the duration of blinks (100 ms) and saccades (20-40 ms).

We investigated whether prematurely born five-year-olds spent less time looking at faces during face-to-face interactions than full-term peers, and whether they look less at the eyes when they do look at a face than full-term peers.
For this, we used a dyadic video-based eye-tracking set-up.

Contrary to our hypothesis, we found no statistically significant group differences in the percentage of total dwell time to face versus background, as well as the eyes versus mouth, between children born preterm compared to those born at term, despite preterm children showing more social difficulties on the ADOS-2.
However, the pattern of this gaze behavior, operationalized by number of dwells per minute and mean dwell duration, does slightly differ between preterm and full-term children.

The absence of a statistically significant group difference between preterm and full-term children in the percentage of total dwell times to the face and eyes can be interpreted in several ways.

Although the findings indicate similar patterns of gaze behavior across groups, a nonsignificant result should not be taken as evidence that the groups did not differ, as smaller effects may have gone undetected.

Nonetheless, one possibility is that, by five years of age, preterm children may no longer differ from full-term peers in the amount of time they spend looking at the face and eyes of their interaction partner, whether this is their mother or a stranger.
This hypothesis is supported by previous work suggesting that early differences in social preferential looking between preterm and full-term infants attenuates by five year of age (37).

text.text: Importantly, they suggested that observed social difficulties may be driven primarily by languagerelated challenges rather than by impairments in visual social orienting.

Consistent with this notion, preterm children in the present study scored significantly lower than full-term peers on the Verbal Comprehension Index and showed significantly more social difficulties as measured by the ADOS-2.
Furthermore, previously reported neural measures from this same cohort demonstrated intact implicit neural tuning to faces in preterm children (42).

text.text: In contrast, group differences were observed in neural tuning to voices, further supporting the notion that the observed social difficulties in preterm children may be more closely related to auditory processing rather than visual attention.

Alternatively, social difficulties in preterm children may not result from atypical social gaze per se, but rather from differences in higher-order processing or interpretation of social information (61).

text.text: Interestingly, we also found small group differences on the number of dwells per minute and mean dwell durations, particularly in eye gaze, with preterm children showing less dwells per minute but longer mean dwell durations than full-term peers.

However, this pattern is in contrast to previous literature reporting more frequent, but shorter moments of social gaze reminiscent of immature attention skills or a self-regulating strategy (29, 32, 33).

text.text: If these group differences reflect a true difference in gaze behavior, we could speculate that preterm children may find disengaging from a social stimulus more difficult.
Previous research indeed suggests that toddlers with a lower gestational age are slower to disengage and shift their attention between different stimuli (62).
text.formatted: Previous research indeed suggests that toddlers with a lower gestational age are slower to disengage and shift their attention between different stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(62)</ref>.

text.text: On the other hand, it is important to note that the effect sizes of these detected group differences between preterm and full-term children are very small.

Furthermore, an important consideration is that the group differences during the silent looking tasks no longer persist when specifically excluding children with significant autism traits from the analyses.
In sum, the groups did not differ significantly in the percentage of total dwell time directed toward faces or eyes, however, differences were observed in other dimensions of gaze behavior.
Specifically, children born preterm showed fewer dwells per minute and longer mean dwell durations.
These findings suggest that similar overall looking time may coexist with differences in the temporal organization of visual attention.
However, the functional significance of these differences remains uncertain and requires further investigation.
An important consideration when interpreting these findings relative to previous research is the time period during which each cohort was observed.
Most studies reporting reduced gaze to faces in preterm infants during face-to-face interactions were conducted no later than 2012 (29) (30) (31) (32).
text.formatted: Most studies reporting reduced gaze to faces in preterm infants during face-to-face interactions were conducted no later than 2012 <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(29)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(30)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(31)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(32)</ref>.

text.text: Another explanation for the absence of group differences in total dwell durations between preterm and full-term children is that our experimental set-up and task design may not have been sufficiently sensitive to capture differences in overall social gaze behavior.

Previous research reporting differences in social gaze behavior in face-to-face interactions between preterm and full-term children showed a pattern of shorter but more frequent gazes to faces (29, 32, 33).
text.formatted: Previous research reporting differences in social gaze behavior in face-to-face interactions between preterm and full-term children showed a pattern of shorter but more frequent gazes to faces <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(29,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">32,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">33)</ref>.

text.text: These studies suggested that immature visual attention mechanisms could be underlying this atypical social gaze pattern.
Our approach suggested a different pattern of less frequent but longer dwells.

However, careful interpretation is warranted as the effect sizes of the group differences were small and our set-up may have been limited in detecting gaze aversions, as no eye-tracking data were available when children gazed away from the screen.
As a result, our analyses were restricted to dwells occurring on the screen, which were either classified as either directed to facial features or elsewhere on the screen.

Although we estimated time spent gazing outside the box set-up (i.e. away from the screen) based on their head orientation measures, these estimates did not differ significantly between groups and showed substantial individual variability.
One way to reduce information loss of 'gazing away from the target' would be to use mobile eye-tracking glasses.
However, this approach introduces additional challenges, including more complex and time-intensive data analysis, particularly with respect to defining AOIs.
A further methodological consideration concerns the definition of facial AOIs.
In the current study, face-related AOIs (eyes, nose and mouth) were large, as recommended by Hessels et al. (2016) (54).
text.formatted: In the current study, face-related AOIs (eyes, nose and mouth) were large, as recommended by Hessels et al. (2016) <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(54)</ref>.

text.text: This is advantageous for noisy data, such as the current eye-tracking data including children in multiple face-to-face interactions.
However, the downfall of such large AOIs is that it limits more spatially fine-grained assessments.
For example, gazes toward the eyebrows or forehead are currently attributed to the eye region.
Although it is technically possible to define separate, smaller AOIs, the spatial accuracy of the eye-tracking data would also need to be substantially better to resolve gaze to such smaller AOIs.
Thus, the current AOI set is most appropriate for the quality of our eye-tracking recordings.
Relatedly, earlier studies that reported group differences in overall face gaze relied on manual video-coding rather than eye-tracking.
As a result, such research investigates gaze behavior to the face more globally, whereas we focused on specific facial features.
This is an important distinction, as the eyes and mouth can be considered as among the most relevant facial features during interactions and conversations (11, 73, 74).
text.formatted: This is an important distinction, as the eyes and mouth can be considered as among the most relevant facial features during interactions and conversations <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">73,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">74)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, while video-coding offers flexibility, it is inherently more subjective and biased than using an eye-tracking system (75-77).

For example, gaze directed broadly to the interaction partner may be coded as face gaze even when fixation is actually directed toward non-facial regions such as hair or body, potentially inflating estimates of face looking and contributing to false positives.
Finally, experimental context itself may have influenced gaze behavior.
Interactions took place in a rather empty room, with bare, white walls.
Positioned behind the box set-up, children were exposed to very limited distractions and the only salient stimulus was the face of their interaction partner.

In contrast, previous studies, especially those using free-play interactions (29, 30, 32), typically provided richer environments with more meaningful ways to disengage from the interaction partner (for example, by looking at toys or surrounding objects).
text.formatted: In contrast, previous studies, especially those using free-play interactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(29,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">30,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">32)</ref>, typically provided richer environments with more meaningful ways to disengage from the interaction partner (for example, by looking at toys or surrounding objects).

text.text: The lab setting and lack of potential distractors may have influenced the children's behavior, promoting sustained visual engagement with the interaction partner.
Also in regard to the small group differences in number of dwells per minute and mean dwell durations, it is important to consider the interactional context and dynamics between partners.

The current research does not take into account for example turn-taking behavior, which may potentially explain individual and group differences in the observed social gaze patterns particularly relevant for eye gaze.
It would be interesting to assess whether similar results would be observed in more unrestricted settings, while also considering the conversational dynamics.

However, such contexts, particularly those employing mobile eye-tracking glasses, pose additional methodological challenges, including reduced precision in facial features discrimination and potential gaze biases introduced by the presence of eye-tracking glasses on the interaction partner in case of dual eye-tracking approaches (78).
text.formatted: However, such contexts, particularly those employing mobile eye-tracking glasses, pose additional methodological challenges, including reduced precision in facial features discrimination and potential gaze biases introduced by the presence of eye-tracking glasses on the interaction partner in case of dual eye-tracking approaches <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">(78)</ref>.

text.text: Although no group differences were observed in percentage of total dwell times, nor an effect of interaction type when children interacted with their mother, we did observe a small effect of interaction partner during the silent looking tasks.
First, all children proportionately gazed more toward their mother's face than toward the face of a female stranger.
This was expected, as previous literature has also reported preferential gaze toward the mother's face versus a stranger's face (79, 80).
text.formatted: This was expected, as previous literature has also reported preferential gaze toward the mother's face versus a stranger's face <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">(79,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">80)</ref>.

text.text: Surprisingly, when assessing eye-versus-mouth gaze, children proportionally gazed more toward the eyes of a stranger than toward the eyes of their mother.

One potential explanation is that children may feel more shy when asked to look at a stranger, which somewhat counter-intuitively has been shown to result in increased eye gaze during face scanning (81, 82).
text.formatted: One potential explanation is that children may feel more shy when asked to look at a stranger, which somewhat counter-intuitively has been shown to result in increased eye gaze during face scanning <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">(81,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">82)</ref>.

text.text: An alternative explanation relates to the behavior of the adult interaction partner during the silent looking task.
Although both mothers and strangers were given the same instructions ("Look at each other without any verbal interaction"), the nonverbal behavior differed considerably.

Prior to the task, both mothers and strangers were instructed that they were allowed to shortly react to nonverbal initiatives of the children (e.g. making a silly face) but not to initiate such nonverbal behavior themselves.

Female strangers (i.e. experimenters) strictly adhered to these instructions, resulting in minimal nonverbal interaction in stranger-child dyads (i.e. both child and stranger mostly maintained neutral expressions).
In contrast, mother-child interactions contained substantially more nonverbal engagement including smiling, laughing, sticking out tongues, and making other silly faces.
These expressive behaviors may have biased children's gaze toward their mother's mouth, since gaze to happy or smiling faces is often characterized by enhanced mouth gaze (83) (84) (85).
text.formatted: These expressive behaviors may have biased children's gaze toward their mother's mouth, since gaze to happy or smiling faces is often characterized by enhanced mouth gaze <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">(83)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">(84)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">(85)</ref>.

text.text: Certain limitations should be considered when interpreting the findings of our study.
First of all, gaze behavior is very individual-dependent, meaning that each individual has their own preferential gaze pattern (86) (87) (88) (89).
text.formatted: First of all, gaze behavior is very individual-dependent, meaning that each individual has their own preferential gaze pattern <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">(86)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">(87)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">(88)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">(89)</ref>.

text.text: This complicates the interpretation of gaze behavior, especially at a group level, and makes it harder to detect overall group differences.

Second, the preterm population is markedly heterogeneous in gestational age, ranging from late to extremely preterm, and in neurodevelopmental outcomes, which span from typical development to subclinical or even severe difficulties, with some children already diagnosed with ASD.
Excluding children with significant autism traits attenuated the detected group differences solely in eye gaze during the silent looking tasks, whereas most findings remained unchanged.
Intelligence scores and autism traits mostly did not differ between the different degrees of prematurity (see Supplementary Materials).

It is also important to note that ten preterm children did not interact with the female stranger (six through excessive crying or repeatedly refusing, and four due to no parental consent for this part of the study), whereas all full-term children completed the stranger interaction.
Moreover, a total of 25 preterm children had to be excluded either due to technical failure (N = 11) or due to poor eye-tracking quality (N = 14).

Although included and excluded preterm children did not significantly differ on general characteristics, this may still have led to a selection bias, including only preterm children willing to complete the tasks and adhering to the instructions such as sitting as still as possible for proper data quality.
This is particularly relevant given that the six preterm children who refused themselves on average had lower scores for Working Memory.
Moreover, 50% of the refusing preterm children showed clinical traits of autism.
The results of the current study should thus be interpreted with caution when trying to generalize to the whole preterm population.
Third, gaze behavior is highly task dependent and viewing patterns differ between for example a silent free viewing task and a conversation.
Even within conversations, a large variability can arise depending on the topic (90) and whether a person is speaking or listening (39, 40).
text.formatted: Even within conversations, a large variability can arise depending on the topic (90) and whether a person is speaking or listening <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(39,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">40)</ref>.

text.text: Variability in gaze behavior may also emerge depending on the interaction partner, even when task instructions are identical.

This was particularly evident when comparing children's gaze behavior toward their mother versus a stranger, resulting in a significant effect of interaction partner on the percentage of gaze to the eyes.
This points to another limitation that is particularly relevant for the study of unrestricted face-to-face interactions, namely that, it leaves participants with a lot of freedom.
This freedom may translate into variability in behavior and topics of discussion, which might in turn complicate the interpretation of results.
Fourth, the cross-sectional design does not allow us to draw conclusions about how this similar total social gaze duration between preterm and full-term children developed by five years of age.
Future research should investigate whether improvements in medical care at NICU and interventions such as NIDCAP have led to enhanced social gaze, even in infancy.
Alternatively, future work could examine whether overall social gaze differs between preterm and full-term infants early on, and gradually converges throughout late infancy and early childhood.

Lastly, it is important to note that our video-based interaction set-up is specifically engineered to capture eye-tracking data with high spatial accuracy while preserving the face-to-face social experience.
Participants view full-frontal video recordings of one another, with the partner's eyes rendered in a position that aligns precisely with the camera located behind the half-silvered mirror.
This configuration ensures that when participants look directly at the screen, they also appear to establish direct eye contact with their interaction partner.
A limitation of this set-up is that the face-to-face interaction is physically restricted by the equipment positioned between participants.
As a result, participants were unable to touch each other, and there was little opportunity for distractions or object-based interactions.
We did, however, estimate the amount of time children spent gazing away from the screen based on head rotation, and this did not differ between preterm and full-term children.

In this sample, preterm and full-term five-year-olds showed no statistically significant differences in total social gaze duration directed toward faces or eyes, although subtle differences were observed in other gaze measures, including less frequent dwells with a longer mean duration in preterm children.

Speculatively, these findings may reflect a developmental catch-up in overall visual social orienting during early childhood, potentially as a result of advances in medical care at NICU primarily with a strong focus on infant neurodevelopment.

However, the results of the current study should be interpreted with caution as our methodological approach vastly differed from that of previous research and allowed for considerable inter-individual variability.

Future research with larger samples should adapt longitudinal designs to assess the developmental trajectory of social gaze over time, and apply consistent methodological approaches across measurement points to minimize potential confounding effects.

Since then, neonatal intensive care practices have changed substantially.

The preterm children in the current study were born between 2016-2018, during a period in which the focus of NICU care has increasingly shifted from survival alone toward optimizing infant well-being and long-term developmental outcomes.
Contemporary NICU interventions place strong emphasis on improving socio-communicative development, particularly through enhancing the parent-infant bond.
Examples include the Family Nurture Intervention (FNI) (63-65) and the Newborn Individualized Developmental Care and Assessment Program (NIDCAP) (66-68).

The preterm children in this sample received care in a NICU that integrates NIDCAP principles into standard clinical practice and is staffed by NIDCAP-trained professionals, and approach that has been associated with improved long-term socio-communicative outcomes (69-71).

In line with this, Aija et al. (2024) found that greater exposure to parental speech during neonatal care was associated with stronger face preference later in infancy among children born preterm (72).
It is thus plausible that early developmental care practices may have contributed to the absence of a group difference in overall social gaze behavior at preschool age, as observed in our study.
